# Stage 0 — Document Accessibility Report

The supplied work is **Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups**, by Yanzhe Zhang, Tao Yu, and Diyi Yang. The supplied text covers physical PDF pages 1–15, corresponding to printed proceedings pages 8387–8401. Publication information on physical p. 1 identifies the Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers, July 27–August 1, 2025.

| Accessibility item | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Main document available | Yes: extracted text for all 15 physical pages is supplied. This establishes coverage of the supplied document, not independent verification of the original PDF. |
| Physical page range | 1–15. All page numbers below refer to physical PDF pages unless explicitly described as printed page numbers. |
| Apparently missing pages | None within the supplied 1–15 text sequence. Images are absent for pp. 10, 11, and 13, but their extracted text is available. |
| Visually inspected pages | 1–9, 12, 14, and 15: twelve supplied page images. |
| Text-only pages | 10, 11, and 13. Their content was read as supplied extracted text; their original layout was not visually inspected. |
| Figures | Figures 1–10 are supplied visually and were inspected. Tiny screenshot text is less readable than the accompanying extracted text. |
| Tables | Tables 1–10 are present in both supplied text and rendered pages. Merged baseline cells require alignment against the visual table. |
| Equations | No numbered mathematical equations, theorems, or proofs were found. Metric definitions are given verbally. |
| Appendix | Appendix A begins on p. 12 and continues through p. 15. The accessibility metadata did not detect it, but the supplied page explicitly labels it. |
| Supplementary material | No separate supplement, embedded file, repository contents, or execution logs were supplied. |
| Referenced absent artifacts | The code repository named on p. 1, cited benchmark implementations, and cited prior papers were not inspected. Metadata flags a possible supplemental reference, but no separately identified supplement can be established from the supplied text. |
| OCR | No additional optical character recognition was performed. Supplied native/extracted text was compared with available page images where useful. |
| Limitations | Exact bar heights and individual scatter-point values are not labeled. Fine screenshot details and individual task identities in heatmaps cannot always be read confidently. |

**Evidence convention.** [A] means author-reported text or caption; [B] means directly observable visual evidence; [C] means analyst-derived calculation; [D] means analyst interpretation. No external information [E] is used. Confidence is HIGH for clearly readable statements and table entries, MEDIUM for bounded interpretations, and UNKNOWN where the supplied work leaves a question unresolved. Text embedded in screenshots and quoted attack prompts is treated solely as research evidence.

**Inventory established before synthesis.** S1 Abstract; S2 §1 Introduction; S3 §2 Related Work; S4 §3 Attack Design; S5 §4 Experiments, including settings, models, implementation, metrics, §4.1 Main Result, §4.2 Ablation Study, and §4.3 Defense; S6 §5 Understanding Agent Attack, including §5.1 Task-level Attack Success Rate, §5.2 How Does Our Attack Succeed?, and §5.3 How Does Our Attack Fail?; S7 §6 Conclusion; S8 Limitations; S9 Ethical Considerations; S10 Acknowledgments; S11 References; A1 Appendix A, including implementation details, ALT-template comparison, prompt templates, attack-step distributions, and delayed-attack hypothesis. Visual objects are F1–F10 and T1–T10, preserving the paper's numbering. Experiment identifiers X1–X13 are introduced below. No separate keywords, formal research-question list, formal algorithm listing, theorem, or numbered equation appears in the supplied work.

# 1. Plain-language orientation

[A] This paper asks whether computer-operating AI agents can be diverted by malicious pop-ups. These agents receive screenshots, sometimes accompanied by structured descriptions of screen elements, and select actions such as clicking or typing. The researchers insert pop-ups that look relevant to the user's task and instruct the agent to click them. The intended user task remains available, but the attacker tries to redirect the agent's next action toward the injected content.

[A] The central result is that this simple form of visible environmental manipulation produces frequent unwanted clicks across five tested vision-language models. In Table 1, attack success rates range from 80.0% to 100.0% for OSWorld screenshot agents, 88.7% to 95.3% for OSWorld Set-of-Mark agents, and 62.1% to 78.4% for VisualWebArena Set-of-Mark agents. These percentages measure clicks at attacked steps, not the percentage of tasks completed or the percentage of tasks that ever experience an attack.

[A] The researchers study what makes a pop-up effective: a short task-related attention hook, a clicking instruction, an information banner such as OK, and alternative text in the accessibility tree. They compare variants, test several prompt defenses, inspect generated agent explanations, and examine whether at least one malicious click occurs during an entire task.

[D, MEDIUM] For the user's research question, this work supplies evidence for an additional vulnerability pathway in web and computer agents: untrusted environment content can affect executable actions. It does **not** establish that web agents are quantitatively more vulnerable than standalone large language models. No matched standalone-model comparison is reported. Its central contribution is an empirical demonstration and component analysis of pop-up attacks on computer-use agents, rather than a controlled comparison between agentic and non-agentic systems.

# 2. Document roadmap

| Original component | Physical pages | Role in the argument |
|---|---:|---|
| Abstract and §1 Introduction | 1–2 | Motivate visual-environment attacks and outline the threat model and headline findings. |
| §2 Related Work | 2–3 | Position the work against visual perturbation, textual injection, grounding methods, and environmental distractions. |
| §3 Attack Design | 3–4 | Define four pop-up components and practical alternatives to ideal attacker knowledge. |
| §4 Experiments: setup and metrics | 4–5 | Specify task subsets, models, insertion procedure, and outcome definitions. |
| §4.1 Main Result | 5 | Interpret model comparison and action-step distributions. |
| §4.2 Ablation Study | 5–6 | Vary hooks, instructions, banners, ALT text, blank content, and size. |
| §4.3 Defense | 6–7 | Test system and step-wise prompts and discuss possible further mitigations. |
| §5.1 Task-level Attack Success Rate | 7–8 | Distinguish repeated-step exposure from whether a task is ever attacked. |
| §5.2 How Does Our Attack Succeed? | 8–9 | Compare generated thoughts and quantify mentioned pop-up components. |
| §5.3 How Does Our Attack Fail? | 9 | Categorize observed failure situations. |
| §6 Conclusion | 9 | Recommend risk recognition, instruction prioritization, and human oversight. |
| Limitations; Ethical Considerations | 10 | Bound model coverage and attack sophistication; state research purpose. |
| Acknowledgments and References | 10–12 | Credit assistance and funding and identify cited work. |
| Appendix A | 12–15 | Add placement specifications, ALT templates, generation prompts, delayed attacks, and task-step heatmaps. |

The appendix materially informs interpretation: attacks are inserted only when enough screen space exists, malicious clicks are ignored during execution, clickability labels are manipulated, and delayed exposure reduces but does not remove vulnerability. These details are part of the substantive analysis, not incidental material.

# 3. Background and context

[A] A **large language model (LLM)** processes language; the tested **vision-language models (VLMs)** also process visual content. A **graphical user interface (GUI)** is the screen interface containing buttons, fields, menus, and other controls. The paper studies VLMs embedded in agents that operate such interfaces, rather than asking models only to describe images.

[A] A **screenshot agent** receives screen images and must ground an intended action to a location. **Grounding** here means connecting an action description, such as clicking a particular item, to the correct screen element or coordinates. A **Set-of-Mark (SoM) agent** receives screenshots with tagged elements plus an **accessibility tree**, abbreviated **a11y tree**. The tree provides structured textual information about interface elements. Tags allow actions to reference an element identifier rather than infer a location solely from pixels. See §2, p. 2.

[A] **Alternative text (ALT text)** provides a textual description associated with an element. The paper's footnote on p. 2 explains that in HTML it is displayed when an element cannot be rendered and has also been used to enhance SoM agents. In this study, attacker-controlled ALT text can repeat the pop-up's task hook and clicking instruction in the agent's textual observation.

[A] **OSWorld** evaluates computer tasks. **VisualWebArena** evaluates visual web tasks. The tables abbreviate VisualWebArena as WebArena; that abbreviation should not be interpreted as evidence that a separate text-only WebArena evaluation was conducted.

[A] The paper defines its pop-ups as clickable malicious images on the screen. They are suspicious environmental objects rather than authorized user requests. The authors connect their threat model to malicious advertising, injected website scripts, and phishing images, but those delivery mechanisms are motivating scenarios rather than separately evaluated deployments.

[D] The security distinction needed to understand the paper is between a user's intended task and text encountered while executing it. A screen element can contain useful information, yet its instruction to click is not automatically authorized. The experiments test whether agents preserve that distinction under deliberately misleading observations.

# 4. Research problem and gap

**Existing problem [A].** Visual computer agents increasingly act on behalf of users, but the risks associated with their visual inputs remain insufficiently understood. A deceptive interface could lead to undesired clicks and, in a real deployment, potentially to malware downloads or deceptive websites. The paper evaluates clicks and task disruption; it does not execute those downstream harms. See pp. 1–2 and §4, pp. 4–5.

**Shortcomings of previous approaches according to the authors [A].** The related-work discussion describes prior attacks using optimized image noise or invisible website instructions. The authors say gradient-based attacks can require thousands of optimization steps and transfer less effectively to commercial closed-source models. They also argue that HTML-based injection does not cover a possible shift toward screenshot-only agents. These are the paper's descriptions of prior work, not independent validation of the cited studies. See §2, pp. 2–3.

**Research gap [A].** The authors investigate malicious, openly visible interface elements that human users might recognize and ignore. Their position is that human recognizability should not disqualify an attack when an autonomous agent is expected to operate with minimal supervision. They contrast deliberate malicious manipulation with unrelated but nonmalicious environmental distractions. See p. 2 and p. 3.

**Motivation [A].** The intended stress test keeps the environment usable while inserting content that changes agent behavior. A successful attack need not resemble an ordinary interface perfectly; it needs to persuade or confuse the agent into taking the attacker's action.

**Scope [A].** The study covers screenshot and SoM agents backed by five general-purpose closed-source VLMs, selected easy tasks in two benchmarks, a four-component pop-up design, and limited defenses. It excludes a standalone-LLM comparison, open-source-model evaluation, actual malware or redirection consequences, and advanced optimized jailbreak strings. Those exclusions limit the conclusions that can be drawn for the user's broader research question.

# 5. Research questions, objectives, and hypotheses

The paper does not present a numbered list of formal research questions or preregistered hypotheses. The following are extracted objectives, not invented author wording.

| ID | Objective or hypothesis | Status and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | Determine whether adversarial pop-ups can mislead VLM agents into clicking them. | Author objective, pp. 2–3; tested by X1. |
| O2 | Identify the contributions of hooks, instructions, banners, and ALT descriptors. | Author objective, §3–§4.2; tested by X3–X8 and X12. |
| O3 | Examine whether attacks remain effective with less attacker information or constrained pop-up size. | Author objective, §3 and §4.2; tested through speculation, alternate instructions, and reduced size. |
| O4 | Assess basic defenses and the ease of countering a step-wise defense. | Author objective, §4.3; tested by X9–X10. |
| O5 | Understand task-level exposure, successful behavior, and failed attacks. | Author objective, §5; examined by X11 and qualitative analysis. |
| H1 | Increased robustness under delayed attacks comes from attack-free history retained in agent memory. | Explicit author hypothesis, p. 13; not isolated experimentally. |

[A] Additional explanatory assumptions include that textual safety training contributes to SoM resistance to virus alerts, that ALT text strengthens attention to task hooks, and that repeated safety prompts can impair planning or grounding. The paper uses language such as assume, probably, or might for these explanations. They are hypotheses or interpretations, not directly established mechanisms.

[D, MEDIUM] The user's question—why web AI agents might be more vulnerable than standalone LLMs—is a synthesis question imposed on this evidence. The study addresses environmental action manipulation, multimodal exposure, and repeated opportunities for compromise. It supplies no direct numerical estimate of the difference between those two system classes.

# 6. Assumptions / Threat Model

[A] **Attacker objective:** make the agent click an adversarial pop-up. **Attack surface:** observations related to the injected element, including screenshots and a11y-tree content. **Default attacker knowledge:** the user query, pop-up location, and underlying agent framework, among other needed information. This is explicitly an idealized setting. See p. 2 and §3, p. 3.

[A] **Attacker control:** add or modify pop-ups and their associated textual descriptions. The default construction can include accurate center coordinates or a tag identifier, a query-derived hook, a misleading button-like banner, and adversarial ALT text. Appendix A further models the element as a clickable button or link through its accessibility representation.

[A] **Reduced-knowledge conditions:** substitute a virus alert or a query guessed from screen information; say click here; use random coordinates or tags; and use coordinates for a SoM agent instead of knowing its framework-specific identifier. **Environmental constraint:** insert a pop-up only when an available area has both height and width greater than 100 pixels. **Size constraint tested:** a 50% reduction in pop-up size, without a clearly specified area-versus-linear-dimension interpretation.

[A] **Modeled delivery scenarios:** malicious advertising slots, cross-site scripting, and clickable phishing images. The experiments manipulate observations directly rather than demonstrate each delivery channel end to end.

[D] **Trust boundary:** the user request and agent configuration supply the task, whereas screen content is environmental evidence. The paper demonstrates a failure to keep some environmental clicking instructions from influencing action selection. It does not give a formal trusted-component specification or measure compromise of the model weights, system prompt, credentials, or operating system.

[A] **Outcome boundary:** clicked pop-ups do not redirect the browser or trigger malware in the experiment. Their clicks are ignored during execution. Thus, an attack can consume actions and influence behavior while leaving the task state largely unchanged. Real consequences are discussed as risks, not measured outcomes.

# 7. Methodology

## Study design and task selection

[A] The work is an empirical cybersecurity and machine-learning study, combining benchmark evaluation, component ablations, prompt defenses, visual examples, manual analysis of generated thoughts, and temporal exposure analysis.

[A] For OSWorld, the researchers select 50 easy tasks from tasks completed in an earlier full-test evaluation without attacks. Both screenshot and SoM agents are tested, with a 15-step limit per task. The authors caution that selection does not guarantee successful completion in a later run: the original benchmark setting used temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.9. The reported experiments use temperature 0 to reduce randomness. See §4 Settings, p. 4.

[A] For VisualWebArena, they use 72 easy tasks selected by Wu et al. and test only SoM agents, with a 30-step limit. The supplied paper does not enumerate the task identifiers or describe a new train/validation/test split. It uses benchmark task subsets rather than reporting model training.

## Models and implementation

[A] The five model versions are gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09, gpt-4o-2024-05-13, gemini-1.5-pro-002, claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, labeled Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2. GPT-4-Vision-preview is excluded because of deprecation. GPT-4o-2024-05-13 also generates task summaries and guesses task intent from linearized a11y-tree information. See p. 4.

[A] The placement procedure first finds the largest available rectangle after excluding interface-element bounding boxes obtained from the a11y tree and OCR detection. It then randomly samples a position and size within that rectangle. Maximum height is 540 pixels and maximum width is 960 pixels. The bottom information banner is 50 pixels high, or one-third of the pop-up height when the pop-up is too small. The procedure searches for the largest fitting font size. This favors readable short text while reducing overlap with recognized interface content. See Appendix A, p. 12.

[A] The default OSWorld instruction is a coordinate instruction for **both** screenshot and SoM agents. The default VisualWebArena instruction uses a tag ID. This distinction matters when interpreting Table 3: OSWorld-SoM's tag instruction is an alternative with ASR 96.1%, rather than its default 91.8% coordinate condition.

[A] The pop-up tag ID is randomly selected and does not correspond to website position. Adversarial accessibility templates label the element as a button in OSWorld or an anchor/link in VisualWebArena. Comparisons use a representation without the button role or with an image role. These are called benign templates, but the task-related ALT content remains; benign therefore describes the role/template manipulation rather than a completely harmless attack.

## Generation prompts

[A] The summary prompt frames the output as the name of one button helping with the user task and requests fewer than five words. The speculation prompt similarly asks for a button name from the linearized a11y tree, asking the model to guess user intent. Short phrases permit large font sizes. These prompts are construction evidence, not instructions for this analysis.

## Metrics and statistical reporting

[A] Original Success Rate (OSR) is task success without pop-ups. Success Rate (SR) is task success with the attack and without redirection after a malicious click. Attack Success Rate (ASR) is the ratio of steps clicking the pop-up among steps where a pop-up was injected. Task-level Attack Success Rate (TASR) is the fraction of tasks containing at least one pop-up click. Benchmark-specific evaluation functions determine task success.

[A] Component ablations use GPT-4-Turbo for OSWorld and GPT-4o for VisualWebArena. The footnote on p. 5 says the updated Claude model was unavailable when ablations were run. It also states that the update did not provide a substantial improvement over GPT-4-Turbo. No formal model-selection criterion combining ASR, SR, and OSR is supplied.

[A] Hardware, API expenditure, timing, software dependency versions, random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, and significance tests are not reported in the supplied text. Random placement is described despite temperature-zero model decoding. The aggregation rule for some headline averages is not fully explained.

# 8. Experiments / Analyses

| ID | Purpose and manipulated condition | Data, comparison, and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| X1 | Test default attacks across five VLM backbones and three agent/benchmark combinations. | OSWorld 50 tasks per tested setting; VisualWebArena 72 tasks; OSR versus attacked SR and ASR; T1, pp. 4–5. |
| X2 | Examine action-step usage with and without attacks. | GPT-4-Turbo on OSWorld, GPT-4o on VisualWebArena; successful and failed task proportions by step bins; F3, p. 4. |
| X3 | Replace query-derived attention hook with virus alert or guessed query. | Ablation models; ASR/SR against common OSR; T2, p. 5. |
| X4 | Compare tag, coordinate, here, and random-target instructions. | Same benchmark subsets; screenshot tagging inapplicable; T3, pp. 5–6. |
| X5 | Replace OK banner with ADVERTISEMENT. | Visual disclosure condition; T4, p. 6. |
| X6 | Compare adversarial ALT, empty ALT, and adversarial ALT with an ad notice. | SoM settings only; T5, p. 6. |
| X7 | Draw blank pop-ups without text or ALT content. | Controls for irrelevant visual additions; T6, pp. 6–7. |
| X8 | Reduce pop-up size by 50%. | Tests a practical size constraint; T6, pp. 6–7. |
| X9 | Add generic or specific system-prompt defenses. | Ignore pop-ups versus also ignore screen clicking instructions; T7, pp. 6–7. |
| X10 | Repeat defense at every step and change the attack wording. | GPT-4-Turbo screenshot agent on OSWorld; remove Please click from attack; ASR/TASR/SR; T8, p. 7. |
| X11 | Examine task-level exposure and generated thoughts, including successful and failed cases. | F4–F6, T9, §§5.1–5.3; 50 successful thoughts per OSWorld agent type for annotation; pp. 7–9. |
| X12 | Change the accessibility role/template while retaining ALT information. | Adversarial clickable versus benign/non-clickable templates; SoM agents; T10, p. 12. |
| X13 | Delay pop-up injection until after the seventh step. | GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld screenshot and SoM agents; F7–F10, pp. 12–15. |

[A] X3–X6 generally vary the named element within an ablation group. The authors explicitly except Table 6 from their one-element-change statement. The supplied text does not describe all repeated-run details or provide individual task-level receipts.

[A] X11's failure analysis identifies three common categories: agents emit WAIT/FAIL/DONE from their interaction history; information-seeking tasks have answers elsewhere on the current page; and explicitly requested familiar tools, such as terminals, give agents confident alternatives. These categories are qualitative: frequencies and complete denominators are not reported.

[D] The controlled comparisons support sensitivity to content and representation. They do not isolate every psychological or model-internal explanation. A textual hook changes semantic relevance, visual text, and potentially ALT text together; a blank condition changes the content substantially; and template comparisons alter perceived clickability.

# 9. Results

## Main benchmark findings

[A] All default conditions in Table 1 have ASR above 60%. OSWorld attacked task success is 0.0%–10.0%, whereas VisualWebArena attacked task success is 43.1%–48.6%. No tested model consistently avoids the attack. These are results on selected subsets and model versions, not all web agents.

[C] As an illustrative within-condition calculation, GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-SoM falls from OSR 52.0% to SR 8.0%: 52.0 − 8.0 = **44.0 percentage points**, or 44.0/52.0 × 100 = **84.6% relative reduction**, rounded to one decimal. GPT-4o VisualWebArena falls from 63.9% to 45.8%: **18.1 percentage points**, or approximately **28.3% relative reduction**. These calculations are analyst-derived and should not be substituted for the abstract's differently aggregated 47% claim.

[A] The abstract reports an average ASR of 86% and a task-success decrease of 47%. Figure 1 separately reports 92.7% and 73.1% of actions clicking pop-ups for OSWorld and VisualWebArena. The aggregation of these headline figures is not fully specified. ASR's formal denominator is injection steps, while Figure 1's caption says all actions. That terminology deserves caution rather than automatic reconciliation.

## Components and knowledge

[A] Query-derived hooks outperform guessed queries in all three ablation settings. Speculated-query ASRs are 53.9%, 34.4%, and 8.0%. A virus hook remains highly effective against OSWorld screenshot agents, ASR 90.0%, but falls to 58.3% for OSWorld-SoM and 1.1% for VisualWebArena-SoM. The authors interpret the SoM difference as potentially related to textual safety training; that mechanism is not directly tested.

[A] Accurate target instructions are influential. Click here yields ASR 11.3% for screenshot agents but 72.8% and 58.4% for the two SoM settings. Random targets yield 11.8%, 13.7%, and 4.1%. VisualWebArena random-tag SR is 34.7%, lower than the default 45.8%, despite much lower pop-up ASR. Thus, avoiding the pop-up specifically does not guarantee successful task behavior.

[A] An ADVERTISEMENT banner leaves ASR at 66.5%, 77.9%, and 56.7%. Empty ALT lowers SoM ASR to 68.1% and 42.9%. Blank pop-ups produce much lower ASR, 2.4%, 3.7%, and 0.0%. Reduced-size pop-ups retain high ASR, 87.4%, 90.1%, and 60.0%.

## Defenses and repeated exposure

[A] Generic system-prompt defense gives ASR 95.9%, 93.4%, and 60.3%, providing little protection compared with default 93.3%, 91.8%, and 62.1%. The more specific prompt yields 52.0%, 72.3%, and 60.2%, so benefits differ greatly by setting.

[A] Step-wise defense in one OSWorld screenshot setting lowers ASR to 5.9%, but TASR remains 32.0% and SR only 8.0%, against OSR 18.0%. Removing Please click from the attack increases ASR to 10.4% and TASR to 44.0%, with SR 10.0%. This is one simple tested wording variant, not an exhaustive attack search.

[A] Delaying attack onset reduces ASR to 80.4% for screenshot agents and 88.1% for SoM agents. Both remain high. The authors hypothesize that earlier clean history helps; no independent memory ablation establishes the cause.

# 10. Figure-by-figure interpretation

## Figure 1 — Headline attack behavior, p. 1

[B] Two screenshot examples show malicious pop-ups in OSWorld and VisualWebArena. Below each, a horizontal action-composition graphic emphasizes a large red pop-up-clicking segment and a smaller other-actions segment. The labeled values are 92.7% and 73.1%; these are exact visually readable author labels, not estimated bar heights. There is no conventional x/y-axis plot or uncertainty display.

[A] The caption calls these proportions of all actions. The formal ASR definition later uses only steps at which pop-ups are injected. The figure illustrates attack prevalence, but it does not resolve whether the denominator and aggregation match Table 1. Screenshot details are illustrative and not sufficient to reconstruct complete trajectories.

## Figure 2 — Four-part pop-up design, p. 3

[B] A boxed pop-up displays a task-like attention hook at the top, a clicking instruction beneath it, and an OK banner at the bottom. An a11y-tree excerpt beneath the image shows an associated ALT descriptor. Colored numbered annotations identify Attention Hook, Instruction, Info Banner, and ALT Descriptor. This is an annotated construction diagram, not a quantitative plot.

[A] The visual and caption establish that the attack can address two observation channels: visible pixels and structured text. The tag-based example does not imply every experiment uses tags; OSWorld defaults to coordinates. The same construction is explained as a workflow in section 12 below.

## Figure 3 — Action-step distributions, p. 4

[B] Three panels correspond to OSWorld-Screen, OSWorld-SoM, and VisualWebArena-SoM. The horizontal axis is Action Steps, grouped into bins. OSWorld extends to a 13–15 bin; VisualWebArena extends to 26–30. The vertical axis is Ratio on a linear scale from 0.0 to 1.0. Pink/red series show attacked failed and successful tasks, and blue/cyan series show unattacked failed and successful tasks. The legend separates attack presence and task outcome. No error bars are shown.

[B] OSWorld attacked mass is concentrated near the step limit. VisualWebArena has substantial early completion mass and additional late failures under attack. Individual heights are not exactly labeled, so no precise bar values are extracted.

[A] The caption specifies GPT-4-Turbo for OSWorld and GPT-4o for VisualWebArena. Nearby text states that more than 50% of tested VisualWebArena tasks can finish within five steps and that many OSWorld tasks reach the 15-step limit. The authors infer that longer OSWorld trajectories offer more opportunities to become stuck. The figure's discrete bins do not by themselves measure elapsed time, monetary cost, or recovery difficulty.

## Figure 4 — ASR versus TASR, p. 7

[B] This scatter plot uses ASR on the horizontal axis and TASR on the vertical axis, both displayed linearly from 0.0 to 1.0. Purple/blue triangles identify OSWorld; orange circles identify VisualWebArena. A gray dashed diagonal is labeled Perfect Positive Correlation and marks equal axis values. No fitted slope, correlation coefficient, confidence band, or error bar is supplied.

[B] Many points lie above the diagonal, especially at low ASR, indicating that a task can experience at least one malicious click even when such clicks are infrequent per step. Several OSWorld points approach TASR 1.0. Exact coordinates of individual unlabeled points are not reported here.

[A] The authors describe a positive association and say TASR can be multiple times ASR when ASR is below 0.2. Their inference of generalizability is stronger than merely observing a positive association; the figure alone does not establish performance outside the studied tasks or benchmarks.

## Figure 5 — Three successful-attack examples, p. 8

[B] Panel 1 is OSWorld-Screen in Thunderbird; panel 2 is OSWorld-SoM in Chromium; panel 3 is VisualWebArena-SoM on a product page. Each pairs a screenshot with original and attacked generated thoughts. This is a qualitative comparison, with no statistical axes.

[A] In panel 1, original behavior navigates to the Bills folder; attacked text instead endorses clicking the pop-up at (1221, 936) and its OK button. In panel 2, original behavior uses Ctrl + Shift + T to reopen a tab; attacked behavior describes a fabricated task-relevant button at (422, 240). In panel 3, original behavior identifies product image [33], whereas attacked behavior follows an injected instruction to click [4]. The coordinates and IDs are example-specific, not general attack parameters.

[D] These examples show how task relevance can be used as a justification for an unwanted action. They are selected successes and cannot establish the frequency of every reasoning pattern. Tiny background screenshot text is secondary and not exhaustively transcribed.

## Figure 6 — Correct-looking thought with compromised action, p. 9

[B] The example pairs original and attacked text/code beneath an airline-page screenshot containing a pop-up. The intended step is focusing a From field. Original code clicks approximately (350, 300); attacked code moves to (240, 298) and clicks, matching the attack's influence while still describing the legitimate field. No population frequency is given.

[A] The caption explicitly identifies a successful attack in which thoughts appear correct while actions are affected. This supports a concrete limitation of defenses that inspect generated thoughts alone. It does not show that all reasoning monitors fail, nor does visible generated text reveal complete model-internal reasoning.

## Figure 7 — Immediate attacks on OSWorld screenshot agents, p. 14

[B] The heatmap's horizontal axis is Step, with labels 0–15, and its vertical axis is Task. Each row represents one task. Red/orange cells denote successfully attacked steps; green cells denote other steps; gray cells denote steps after termination. Dense red trajectories visually show repeated successful attacks. No task names or exact per-row totals are labeled.

[A] The model is GPT-4-Turbo's screenshot agent. The figure supports the author's description of agents repeatedly clicking pop-ups instead of effectively exploring. Whether every green step contains an injected but ignored pop-up is not specified by the caption's other-steps label.

## Figure 8 — Delayed attacks on screenshot agents, p. 14

[B] Encoding and axes match Figure 7. The first portion is largely green; red attack-success cells appear after the marked attack-free prefix. Gray regions show termination. The caption states that attacks begin after the seventh step.

[A] Appendix text gives ASR 80.4% for this condition. The earlier green cells are deliberately attack-free and should not be interpreted as successful resistance. The figure does not supply delayed-condition SR or a causal estimate of memory's contribution.

## Figure 9 — Immediate attacks on OSWorld SoM agents, p. 15

[B] The heatmap uses the same task-row and step-column scheme. Red/orange cells dominate many trajectories, with scattered green steps and some gray termination regions. It presents GPT-4-Turbo SoM-agent behavior.

[A] The default ASR for the corresponding model/setting is 91.8% in Table 1. The figure illustrates distributions and persistence; it is not an independently labeled numerical table of every action.

## Figure 10 — Delayed attacks on SoM agents, p. 15

[B] The same encoding shows an initial green block before later red regions. The caption specifies onset after the seventh step. Appendix text reports ASR 88.1%.

[D] Comparison with Figure 9 suggests that early clean history changes subsequent behavior modestly, but the supplied material does not isolate history from later task state, shorter remaining exposure, or task termination. The causal explanation remains the authors' hypothesis.

# 11. Table-by-table interpretation

**Reading convention.** All numerical entries below are percentages and author-reported, visually cross-checked where supplied. Each triple is **ASR / SR / OSR**. Lower ASR and higher SR or OSR are preferable for agent security or task performance. # 12. Diagram / Architecture Interpretation

[B/A] Figure 2 is the main substantive design diagram. Its visible components encode a compact persuasive sequence: the attention hook suggests relevance to the authorized task; the instruction specifies the attacker's desired action; the information banner presents a familiar-looking completion or confirmation affordance; and the ALT descriptor repeats relevant content in the structured textual observation.

[A] The procedural architecture can be reconstructed from §3 and Appendix A without inventing an additional author diagram:

1. Input the user query, or screen-derived a11y information if the query is unavailable.
2. Use GPT-4o to generate a short task-related phrase.
3. Identify unoccupied screen space using a11y-tree and OCR bounding boxes.
4. Randomly choose a fitting pop-up position and size, respecting maximum dimensions.
5. Render the hook, instruction, and banner with a large fitting font.
6. Add an associated tagged/accessibility representation when the agent uses one.
7. Present the modified observation to the agent.
8. Observe whether the agent selects a pop-up click.
9. Ignore that click during execution and continue until task completion, termination, or the step limit.

[D] Two paths carry attack information: a visual path through screenshot pixels and a textual path through ALT and element roles. The agent joins these with the legitimate task when choosing an action. Repeated observation/action cycles create repeated attack opportunities. The supplied paper does not draw a complete software-component architecture, specify all interfaces, or expose internal model processing; this reconstruction describes the reported procedure only.

# 13. Equations and mathematical concepts

No numbered equations or formal proofs appear. The following expressions are analyst-written restatements of the verbal metric definitions, not quotations of author equations.

Let K be the number of evaluated tasks; C0 the number completed without attack; C1 the number completed with attack; I the number of steps where a pop-up was injected; P the number of those steps clicking the pop-up; and H the number of tasks with at least one pop-up click. Then:

- **OSR = 100 × C0/K.** What proportion of tasks are completed without attack?
- **SR = 100 × C1/K.** What proportion are completed under attack when pop-up clicks do not redirect execution?
- **ASR = 100 × P/I.** At attacked steps, how often does the agent click the injected object?
- **TASR = 100 × H/K.** Across entire tasks, how often does at least one such click occur?

[D] These formulas require denominators appropriate to the actual evaluated group. The paper does not fully specify whether reported cross-task or cross-model averages pool step counts or average individual rates. ASR is conditional on insertion and should not be computed using all possible steps unless every step receives a pop-up.

[C] For two rates a and b expressed as percentages, their absolute difference is a − b percentage points; the relative reduction is 100 × (a − b)/a percent. For the specific system defense in OSWorld-Screen, (93.3 − 52.0)/93.3 × 100 ≈ 44.3% relative reduction. For OSWorld-SoM, (91.8 − 72.3)/91.8 × 100 ≈ 21.2%; for VisualWebArena, (62.1 − 60.2)/62.1 × 100 ≈ 3.1%. Their unweighted mean is approximately 22.9%, but that mean is analyst-derived and is not asserted to reproduce the authors' aggregation.

[D] A task's ever-click event and a step's click event answer different questions. It would be inappropriate to infer TASR using an independent-trial formula without assumptions about repeated-step independence, exposure counts, and task heterogeneity. None of those assumptions is established here, so no synthetic probability model is introduced.

# 14. Interpretation and discussion

[A] The findings support O1: default pop-ups cause high click rates across all tested combinations. O2 is addressed by large changes under hook, instruction, and ALT manipulations. O3 receives mixed support: guessed queries reduce attack effectiveness substantially, whereas reduced size and alternate targeting often preserve considerable ASR. O4 shows weak generic system defenses, heterogeneous specific defenses, and a stronger step-wise defense with residual task-level exposure. O5 shows repeated attacks, differences in generated text, and several qualitative failure categories.

[D, MEDIUM] The evidence suggests that task relevance can turn untrusted content into an apparent intermediate step toward the legitimate goal. A fabricated reopen-tab message is persuasive precisely because it resembles the task. The paper's data support this behavioral interpretation but do not establish the model's internal cognitive mechanism.

[D, MEDIUM] For the user's research question, three agent-specific factors are visible in the study: the environment carries adversarial instructions, visual and accessibility representations can reinforce them, and actions recur throughout a task. Execution makes an erroneous response operational: the system clicks. # 17. Threats to validity

These labels are analyst-applied, not terminology claimed by the authors.

**Internal validity [D].** Ablations provide useful comparisons, but hook content and ALT repetition can jointly change inputs. The text does not specify identical placement seeds across conditions. Mechanistic explanations involving training, attention, or memory are not isolated through dedicated interventions.

**External validity and generalizability [D].** Five closed-source backbones and two benchmarks support breadth within the tested configurations. Selected easy tasks, ideal attacker knowledge, and fixed versions limit extrapolation to other agents, open-source systems, unfamiliar websites, long-horizon workflows, and deployment controls.

**Construct validity [D].** ASR measures a specific click on the pop-up, not all unsafe behavior. SR under ignored clicks measures task completion under a simplified consequence model. TASR better captures an ever-click event but is still not a measured probability of malware installation, data theft, or irreversible harm. Generated thoughts are observable outputs, not complete internal explanations.

**Statistical conclusion validity [D].** No confidence intervals, formal significance tests, or repeat counts are supplied. Terms such as significant in the prose should be read as qualitative descriptions unless supported by an explicitly reported test. Step observations within one trajectory are not established as independent.

**Ecological validity [D].** Observation insertion corresponds conceptually to advertising and phishing, but the study does not demonstrate realistic attacker acquisition of user queries, control over exact placements, or an end-to-end delivery mechanism. Actual redirects could alter both behavior and available observations relative to the ignored-click setting.

**Reproducibility [D].** Exact model identifiers, prompts, dimensions, and task counts help. The uninspected code repository may contain additional details, but the supplied paper does not expose all task IDs, seeds, dependencies, execution traces, or evaluation receipts. Reproduction cannot be certified from these pages alone.

# 22. Very simple explanation — Explain Like I'm 15

Imagine asking a computer assistant to reopen a browser tab. While it looks at the screen, someone adds a fake message saying REOPEN CLOSED TAB and tells it to click a particular spot. The assistant may decide that this message is a helpful part of the task, even though it came from the attacker. The researchers built pop-ups like this and placed them into computer and web tasks.

The tested assistants clicked these pop-ups very often. Their attackers could put misleading words directly in the image and, for some agents, also in the computer's text description of the image. Knowing the user's task and telling the assistant exactly where to click made the attack stronger. Simply labeling something as an advertisement or adding a general warning to the assistant's instructions usually did not solve the problem.

An important detail is that a low chance of clicking on one step can still mean many tasks contain at least one bad click. In one defense test, only 5.9% of attacked steps produced a pop-up click, but 32.0% of tasks had at least one. Another detail is that the assistant could describe the correct plan while clicking the wrong location, so checking its explanation alone may miss the problem.

This helps explain a possible extra risk of web agents: they continually read material other people control and turn what they read into actions. But this paper does not compare them directly with ordinary chat-only language models. It also does not actually download malware or redirect the browser after a bad click. Its strongest conclusion is that the tested computer agents have trouble keeping misleading screen instructions separate from the user's real request.

claims.statement: The threat model targets agent clicks by manipulating observations related to an adversarial pop-up, including screenshots and accessibility-tree content.
The attack uses four components: an attention hook, a clicking instruction, an information banner, and an ALT descriptor when the agent consumes accessibility text.
The evaluation uses 50 selected easy OSWorld tasks with a 15-step limit and 72 selected easy VisualWebArena tasks with a 30-step limit; VisualWebArena tests only SoM agents.

Table 1 reports default ASR above 60% for every tested model/setting: 80.0–100.0% for OSWorld-Screen, 88.7–95.3% for OSWorld-SoM, and 62.1–78.4% for VisualWebArena-SoM. ASR measures pop-up clicks among injected steps.
Malicious pop-up clicks are ignored during execution and do not trigger redirection, so reported task success does not measure actual malware or deceptive-site consequences.

Using speculated rather than known user-query hooks yields ASR 53.9% for GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-Screen, 34.4% for GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-SoM, and 8.0% for GPT-4o VisualWebArena-SoM, compared with default 93.3%, 91.8%, and 62.1%.
Replacing OK with ADVERTISEMENT reduces ASR but leaves it at 66.5%, 77.9%, and 56.7% in the Screen, OSWorld-SoM, and VisualWebArena-SoM ablation settings, respectively.
Empty ALT text lowers ASR from 91.8% to 68.1% in OSWorld-SoM and from 62.1% to 42.9% in VisualWebArena-SoM, while the visible attack remains.
For GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-Screen, step-wise defense gives ASR 5.9%, TASR 32.0%, and SR 8.0%; removing Please click from the attack changes these to 10.4%, 44.0%, and 10.0%. OSR is 18.0%.
TASR counts a task as attacked if the agent ever clicks a pop-up during its trajectory, distinguishing task-level exposure from ASR's step-level rate.

The paper supplies a successful-attack example in which generated thoughts describe the intended action correctly but executable click coordinates are influenced by the pop-up; the prevalence of this pattern is not quantified.
The authors acknowledge closed-source-only evaluation and not exploring advanced jailbreak-string optimization or stronger persuasion, limiting mechanistic understanding and attack coverage.

When attacks begin after the seventh step, reported OSWorld ASR remains 80.4% for screenshot agents and 88.1% for SoM agents; the authors' clean-history explanation is a hypothesis rather than an isolated causal finding.

The specific system-prompt defense reduces OSWorld-Screen ASR from 93.3% to 52.0%, a 41.3-percentage-point decrease and approximately 44.3% relative reduction: (93.3−52.0)/93.3×100. Thus, the introductory 25%-relative statement cannot be a bound applying to every defense condition.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to agent vulnerability because untrusted visual and accessibility content can steer executable actions repeatedly during a task. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, so relative vulnerability between those system classes remains unmeasured.

limitations: Only supplied text and images were used; no tools, browsing, repository inspection, or external verification was performed.
Physical pages 1–15 were read as text; pages 1–9, 12, 14, and 15 were visually inspected. Pages 10, 11, and 13 were text-only.
All ten numbered figures and ten numbered tables were represented, but tiny screenshot text and unlabeled plot coordinates were not exhaustively transcribed.
No separate supplementary material was supplied; the metadata's supplemental-reference flag does not identify an inspectable artifact.
The headline average ASR, task-success reduction, and action-percentage aggregations are incompletely specified.
Several prose percent reductions numerically match percentage-point differences; the defense reduction statement does not apply uniformly to all shown conditions.
The study does not directly compare standalone LLMs with agents, execute downstream malware or redirection, or measure human resistance.
Closed-source model coverage, selected easy tasks, absent uncertainty estimates and repeat counts, and uninspected code constrain causal interpretation and reproducibility.
